His troponin level was normal, and echocardiography revealed normal wall motion. His metabolic panel showed no electrolyte derangements. The ECG inFigure 1B is not typical for pericarditis. The abnormal ECG findings were due to apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles underlying the precordial leads. With application of external pressure to the precordial leads along the intercostal space, ST-segment changes resolved (Figure 2A). Of note, true ST depressions were noted after manual compression (Figure 2A). These ST depressions were thought to be due to profound hypoxia and subendocardial ischemia. The limb leads were also affected in this case because leads II and III were placed on the upper abdomen to avoid entanglement with other lines and tubes. Paralysis of the intercostal muscles likely resulted in direct transmission of the apical impulse to the ECG leads. Review of telemetry showed this ECG change occurring immediately after the patient was intubated and paralyzed. Physical palpation revealed a subtle, left parasternal lift most prominent over lead V4. Pulse-congruent ECG artifacts have been observed with prominent right radial arterial pulsation1and left forearm arteriovenous fistula,2and with left leg arterial pulsations.3These arterial pulse tapping artifacts are also known as the Aslanger sign.4There are no documented cases of artifact caused by apical impulse. The point of maximal impulse (PMI) refers to the location on the chest wall where contractions in systole are best palpated or visually observed, which correlates with the anatomic position of the cardiac apex. In healthy individuals, the PMI typically occurs as a single, unsustained tap for each systolic contraction palpable over a 2- to 3-cm area at the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. With loss of intercostal muscle tension, the cardiac impulse may be more easily transmitted to the apical leads. The patient was eventually placed on venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation due to worsening hypoxic respiratory failure in the setting of multifocal pneumonia and transplant rejection. He was treated with a course of steroids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. He was then decannulated and underwent tracheostomy. He was eventually discharged after a prolonged hospital course.
